name: Treaty with Governor Nicholson
ceded: First recorded Cherokee land cession to British
detail: A Cherokee delegation met with Governor Francis Nicholson of South Carolina, establishing British claims over Cherokee territory. This set the pattern for over a century of land cessions.

name: Treaty of DeWitt's Corner
ceded: Nearly all remaining South Carolina lands
detail: First forced cession after military defeat in the 1776 campaign. Dragging Canoe refused to accept this treaty and established the Chickamauga Cherokee as a breakaway resistance faction.

name: Treaty of Long Island of Holston
ceded: All lands east of Blue Ridge in NC/VA; claims north of Nolachucky River
detail: Settlers immediately violated the new boundaries, a pattern that would repeat with every subsequent treaty.

name: Treaty of Hopewell
ceded: Confirmed prior cessions; first U.S.–Cherokee treaty
detail: The new United States government guaranteed Cherokee lands — then flagrantly violated its own treaty. Over 500 white families settled illegally on Cherokee territory.

name: Treaty of Holston
ceded: All claims east of Clinch River
detail: Introduced the U.S. "civilization program" and a $1,000 annuity. The U.S. promised to "guarantee the remainder forever."

name: Treaty of Tellico
ceded: East TN between Clinch River, Cumberland Plateau, and Tennessee/Little Tennessee Rivers
detail: Again promised to "continue guarantee forever" — broken within six years.

name: Treaties of 1804, 1805, 1806
ceded: Multiple rapid cessions including Federal Road right-of-way
detail: Negotiated by U.S. Agent Return J. Meigs through bribery of individual chiefs. The 1805 treaty included a Federal Road right-of-way through Cherokee territory. Chief Doublehead was killed by fellow Cherokee for selling land without authorization.

name: Treaty of Fort Jackson
ceded: Approximately 4 million acres of Cherokee land (claimed as Creek territory)
detail: Cherokee warriors fought alongside Andrew Jackson as allies at the Battle of Horseshoe Bend. Jackson then demanded Cherokee land anyway, claiming it was Creek territory.

name: Treaties of 1816, 1817, 1819
detail: The 1817 treaty was the first with explicit removal provisions. Approximately 1,500–2,000 Cherokee voluntarily emigrated west. Afterward, the Cherokee Council declared: "Not one more foot of land."

name: Treaty of New Echota
ceded: ALL remaining Cherokee territory east of the Mississippi
detail: Signed by approximately 500 Cherokee out of a nation of 17,000. NOT authorized by the Cherokee government or Principal Chief John Ross. The U.S. Senate ratified it 31–15 — exactly one vote above the two-thirds threshold required. This treaty authorized the forced removal known as the Trail of Tears.
